papers.title: mTOR signalling, not clock gene rhythms, organises daily physiology
papers.abstract: Daily rhythms in mammalian physiology are widely attributed to rhythmic transcription of "clock-controlled genes" driven by the circadian transcriptional/translational feedback loop (TTFL). Here we show that daily physiology can be uncoupled from the TTFL: inhibiting the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) abolishes most daily variation in cellular and organismal physiology, whilst clock protein rhythms persist. In cultured cells and mouse liver, functional rhythms are lost, including the proteome, RNA abundance, substrate utilisation and drug metabolism. In forebrain, most daily variation in protein abundance and phosphorylation is lost, yet locomotor activity and sleep-wake architecture are largely preserved in mice and zebrafish. PERIOD2 binds mTORC1 and limits its activity, providing a route by which clock proteins shape daily mTOR signalling. mTOR inhibition preferentially suppresses output over clock gene rhythms in Arabidopsis and Neurospora. We conclude that mTOR is a conserved conduit through which circadian and environmental timing impose daily organisation on physiology.

Acute mTOR inhibition abolishes functional rhythms in cells and most daily liver physiology, while preserving sleep/wake cycles, and shows evolutionary conservation as a circadian effector across species.

papers.title: Acute sleep deprivation induces ECM-associated transcription and MMP12-sensitive perivascular remodeling.
papers.abstract: Sleep deprivation (SD) disrupts brain homeostasis, but whether acute sleep loss alters extracellular matrix (ECM) programs and the structural organization of the perivascular interface remains unclear. We integrated re-analysis of three public 6-h SD transcriptomic datasets with cisterna magna tracer studies, collagen IV and hyaluronan-binding protein 2 (HABP2) imaging, cellular localization of matrix metalloproteinase-12 (MMP12), transmission electron microscopy, pharmacological MMP12 inhibition, and continuous EEG/EMG recording during ZT0-ZT6 and recovery, with manual sleep-wake scoring in 4-s epochs. Across GSE256140, GSE78215, and GSE128770, acute SD was associated with increased ECM-related transcription. In GSE256140, the most prominent differential response occurred in excitatory neurons, and six of 18 upregulated genes were annotated to the extracellular matrix term. SD increased tracer displacement relative to collagen IV, broadened collagen IV- and HABP2-positive perivascular bands, and expanded an ECM-associated perivascular compartment at the ultrastructural level. Cortical MMP12 immunoreactivity was associated most strongly with NeuN-positive structures, followed by Iba1-positive structures, with limited enrichment in GFAP-positive regions. MMP408 attenuated the SD-associated redistribution of tracer and normalized widening of the perivascular compartment, but did not significantly restore the narrowed endothelial-basement membrane complex. During ZT0-ZT6, rotating-bar SD increased wakefulness and reduced NREM and REM sleep. Recovery NREM sleep was increased in both SD groups, whereas NREM spectral profiles and relative delta power did not differ significantly among the four groups. Acute SD engages an ECM-associated transcriptional response and produces structural reorganization of the perivascular interface. The pharmacological findings identify an MMP12-sensitive component of this remodeling without establishing a single cellular source of MMP12. These results connect sleep loss to ECM and perivascular structural plasticity while separating these changes from the magnitude of early recovery sleep.

ai.summary: Integrated re-analysis of three 6-h sleep deprivation transcriptomic datasets with tracer, imaging, electron microscopy, and pharmacological experiments in mice, showing acute SD increases ECM-related transcription and remodels the perivascular interface. MMP12 inhibition (MMP408) attenuated tracer redistribution and perivascular widening, linking an MMP12-sensitive component to SD-induced structural plasticity without restoring the endothelial-basement membrane complex.

papers.title: Flavonoid chronotherapy normalizes circadian dynamics and sleep architecture in mice with painful nerve injury
papers.abstract: Neuropathic pain (NP) is linked to disrupted sleep and circadian abnormalities upon painful peripheral nerve injury. By performing spared nerve injury (SNI) in circadian reporter PER2::LUC mice, we characterized the real-time changes in rhythmicity of the core clock gene Per2 in the pain-regulating dorsal root ganglia (DRG), and the sleep-wake cycle using wireless EEG/EMG under NP conditions. We further evaluated whether the clock-resynchronizing flavonoids, nobiletin (2 mg/kg/day) and tangeretin (1.8 mg/kg/day), administered continuously via osmotic minipumps for two weeks, could restore circadian dynamics and alleviate pain-related behaviour. Both flavonoids alleviated SNI-induced dynamic hypersensitivity in PER2::LUC mice on post-surgical day 14. SNI increased the amplitude of Per2 rhythms in the DRGs, which was restored to pre-surgical levels by administration of flavonoids. In addition, tangeretin showed sleep-restoring properties upon SNI by alleviating disturbances in NREM sleep and wakefulness. These results support targeting circadian disruption as a potential chronotherapeutic approach to alleviate NP.

papers.title: AnySleep: a channel-agnostic deep learning system for high-resolution sleep staging in multi-center cohorts.
papers.abstract: Sleep is essential for health, yet studying its dynamics requires manual sleep staging, a labor-intensive step in research and clinical care. Across centers, polysomnography (PSG) recordings are traditionally scored in 30-s epochs for pragmatic, not physiological, reasons and vary in electrode count, montage, and subject characteristics. These constraints challenge harmonized multi-center studies and the discovery of robust biomarkers on shorter timescales. We present AnySleep, a deep neural network that scores sleep from any electroencephalography (EEG) or electrooculography (EOG) data at adjustable temporal resolutions. We trained and validated the model on over 20,000 overnight recordings (>200,000 h of EEG and EOG) from 28 datasets across multiple clinics to promote robust generalization across sites. The model attains state-of-the-art performance and surpasses or equals established baselines at 30-s epochs. Performance improves with more channels, yet remains strong when EOG is absent, or only EOG or single EEG derivations (frontal, central, or occipital) are available. On sub-30-s timescales, the model captures short wake intrusions consistent with arousals and improves the prediction of pathophysiological conditions (obstructive sleep apnea, narcolepsy type 1, insomnia) over 30-s scoring. We make the model publicly available to facilitate large-scale studies with heterogeneous electrode setups and accelerate biomarker discovery in sleep.

It attains state-of-the-art 30-s epoch performance, remains strong with single EEG derivations or EOG alone, and at sub-30-s resolution captures short wake intrusions and improves prediction of obstructive sleep apnea, narcolepsy type 1, and insomnia.

papers.title: Characterization of Sleep, Spectral, and Epileptiform Activity in Individuals Aged 8-27 Years with SYNGAP1-Related Disorder Using an at-Home Dry EEG Headband
papers.abstract: SYNGAP1-related disorder (SYNGAP1-RD) is associated with sleep disturbances, seizures, and neurophysiological abnormalities. However, in-lab EEG can be difficult to obtain due to the behavioral and sensory disorders associated with this condition. In this study we collected EEG in SYNGAP1-RD participants (n=30 enrolled, 27 contributing data) in a decentralized protocol using a dry electrode headband as a path to longitudinal, research-grade data collection in this population. At-home data collection was successful with 180 recordings containing over 1 hour of usable data collected from 23 participants. Across these recordings, sporadic interictal epileptiform discharges were present in 22 of 23 participants but electrographic seizures were not observed. Relative to an adolescent control population (n=10), SYNGAP1-RD participants showed increased wake after sleep onset, reduced sleep efficiency, and decreased time in N1 and N3 sleep stages along with increased time in N2. We reproduced prior findings from awake spectral EEG analyses, including elevated broadband power along with reduced relative alpha power and alpha-theta ratio in the SYNGAP1 cohort. Notably, differences in spectral power were tightly linked to sleep stage, revealing sleep-stage-dependent spectral biomarker dynamics not previously characterized in SYNGAP1-RD. Finally, we examined differences between variants producing truncations downstream of the GAP domain and those producing truncations before or within it, but analyses were limited by a small sample size (n=4 for the post-GAP variant). Overall, this study demonstrates the feasibility of at-home multi-night sleep EEG collection in participants with SYNGAP1-RD and led to both corroborative and novel findings.

It also reproduced awake spectral abnormalities and revealed sleep-stage-dependent spectral biomarker dynamics.

papers.title: Capturing the rhythm: methodological choices shape inference from circadian activity data
papers.abstract: Abstract 1. Statistical tools and analytical decisions for analysing animal activity data are often limited and poorly justified, particularly with respect to model choice, sampling design and temporal aggregation. These shortcomings can constrain our ability to draw accurate and biologically meaningful inferences about behaviour. 2. We interrogated 24 h activity data taken from individual males and females derived from five Drosophila melanogaster populations to generate a general framework for collecting and analysing activity data that systematically compares common model classes, continuous verses fragmented sampling strategies, and alternative temporal aggregation choices (time-bin sizes). 3. Our analyses identified generalised additive mixed models (GAMMs) applied to high-frequency continuous data with small-moderate bin sizes (1-5 minutes) as providing the most robust and interpretable inference for our complex, high-frequency activity data. 4. However, our interrogation of the data set confirmed that analytical and sampling decisions need to be tailored to the study species, the timing of activities and the nature of the behaviour of interest. Accordingly, polynomial and cosinor generalised linear models, increased but biologically targeted snapshot sampling, and bin sizes smaller than one hour yielded adequate analyses with similar biological conclusions when appropriately matched to the system. 5. Our approach provides an accessible decision-making framework for activity analyses that allows researchers across behavioural, ecological and evolutionary studies to justify and optimise choices about data collection and modelling. Such an approach improves the biological relevance of inference and supporting the use of modern tracking and analytical technologies.

ai.summary: Used 24-h activity data from individual male and female Drosophila melanogaster across five populations to systematically compare model classes, sampling strategies, and temporal bin sizes. Generalized additive mixed models on high-frequency continuous data with 1-5 minute bins gave the most robust inference, though appropriately matched cosinor/polynomial GLMs, targeted snapshot sampling, and bins under one hour yielded similar biological conclusions.

papers.title: Measuring Sleep at Home in Adolescents With Autism Using EEG Headbands: Protocol for a Remote Study.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances are prevalent in autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) and worsen daytime functioning, yet their neural bases remain poorly understood. This may reflect the challenges of laboratory-based polysomnography for individuals with ASD, including sensory sensitivities and difficulty adapting to changes in routine. The advent of wearable electroencephalography (EEG) devices allows for remote data collection in the home and facilitates large-scale sleep studies. The aim of this study is to test the hypothesis that thalamocortical circuit dysfunction contributes to poor sleep in ASD by characterizing sleep oscillations that rely on this circuitry. To achieve this goal, we monitored sleep in the home using wearable EEG headbands in adolescents with ASD, including those who are profoundly affected, and their typically developing peers. When necessary, we used a desensitization protocol to gradually acclimate participants to wearing the headband overnight to promote the inclusion of individuals with sensory sensitivities and high support needs. Participants and their families completed assessments and questionnaires and received remote training to use a wearable EEG headband. Those needing time to acclimate followed a personalized 2-week desensitization protocol with a practice headband. Sleep was monitored at home for 3 consecutive nights, the first of which was for adaptation to the headband. Sleep data quality was checked daily, and remote technical support was provided as needed. Using sleep rhythms as physiological biomarkers of thalamocortical circuit function, we will test the hypothesis that abnormal circuit function in ASD is related to worse sleep quality. This study was funded by the Simons Foundation Autism Research Initiative (SFARI) and approved by the Mass General Brigham Institutional Review Board in November 2021. Data were collected between July 2023 and November 2025. A total of 146 participants (ASD: n=77; typically developing [TD]: n=65; profound autism: n=4) completed the study and produced at least 1 night of usable sleep data. Data analysis is underway, and the results will be submitted for publication in November 2026. At-home sleep monitoring enables large samples that are needed to characterize the neural underpinnings of sleep disturbances across the autism spectrum. The personalized desensitization protocol promotes inclusion by accommodating individuals often excluded from research due to sensory or behavioral challenges. These methods are adaptable for other conditions and research goals beyond ASD, such as longitudinal studies across development or characterizing sleep in other neurodevelopmental disorders. Desensitization protocols may also increase the tolerability of diagnostic laboratory-based sleep studies and other medical procedures, improving both patient experience and quality of care.

papers.title: An automated EEG-ECG framework for CAP-HRV analysis: enabling brain-heart coupling studies in sleep disorders.
papers.abstract: Multimodal sleep analysis typically requires separate processing pipelines for electroencephalography (EEG) and electrocardiography (ECG), which complicates joint investigation of sleep microstructure and autonomic regulation. Cyclic alternating pattern (CAP) scoring and heart rate variability (HRV) analysis are routinely performed in different software environments, limiting temporal alignment, reproducibility, and scalability. We present an open-source MATLAB framework that integrates rule-based CAP A1 detection and HRV feature extraction within a single, time-synchronized workflow. The pipeline performs standardized EEG and ECG preprocessing, rule-based CAP A1 detection during slow-wave sleep (SWS) implementing the Terzano scoring criteria, R-peak detection via the Pan-Tompkins algorithm, and computation of time-domain, frequency-domain, and nonlinear HRV features by calling the open-source PhysioZoo/mhrv toolbox directly. CAP annotations are aligned with 5-minute ECG epochs through the shared polysomnography (PSG) time base. The complete code is released as an open-source repository to support reuse and extension. Because HRV features are computed by calling the PhysioZoo/mhrv toolbox directly, the pipeline introduces no reimplemented HRV routine and inherits that toolbox's validated feature definitions. CAP A1 detection is provided as a rule-based implementation of published criteria and has not yet been benchmarked against expert manual scoring. A worked example on the OSAD+ subgroup (n = 18) demonstrates pipeline output across CAP and non-CAP epochs, and a healthy-sleep A1-event HRV reference is reported from the public CAP Sleep Database (15 controls, 785 A1 epochs) as a descriptive cross-database reference. The framework provides a reproducible, rule-based, and modular tool for integrated EEG-ECG analysis of sleep microstructure and autonomic dynamics. By enabling synchronized CAP-HRV feature extraction in a single environment, it lowers the engineering barrier to brain-heart coupling research during sleep and provides a foundation for future extensions, including validated CAP detection, a matched-control study, a Python port, and cloud-based deployment.

papers.title: Differential circadian time modulates of dentate gyrus and CA1 excitation-inhibition balance and seizure threshold.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms regulate seizure threshold and neuronal excitability in epilepsy. Temporal lobe seizures tend to arise more frequently during the diurnal phase relative to the nocturnal phase, yet dentate gyrus (DG) granule cells display elevated intrinsic excitability and CA1 pyramidal neurons show enhanced synaptic excitability at night. Here, we used male adult ICR mice (8-10 weeks old) as experimental subjects. Systemic pilocarpine injection was applied to pharmacologically trigger acute seizures, while AAV (pAAV2/9-CaMKIIα-hChR2 (H134R) - EYFP) delivery followed by optogenetic stimulation (10 Hz, 20 ms pulse width, 5 mW 473 nm blue light) was implemented to evoke region-specific hippocampal seizures. Combining continuous video-electroencephalography (vEEG) recording, optogenetically induced seizure assays, mRNA sequencing, and whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology, we investigated circadian modulation of neuronal excitability and seizure threshold within the DG and CA1 subfields of the hippocampus. Our results revealed divergent circadian regulation of seizure thresholds between the DG and CA1 regions. Notably, the diurnal-nocturnal seizure threshold pattern in CA1 recapitulated that seen in systemic pilocarpien-provoked seizure models. We further confirmed that circadian cycles exert distinct regulatory effects on excitatory/inhibitory synaptic transmission and the intrinsic excitability of hippocampal principal neurons in the DG and CA1. Collectively, this work highlights region-specific circadian control over seizure susceptibility and the brain excitation-inhibition balance. Elucidating circadian influences on hippocampal physiology and seizure threshold will improve the translational value of anti-epileptic therapies and guide time-stratified seizure intervention strategies.

papers.title: Motor memory consolidation during sleep after stroke: the rehabilitation timing hypothesis.
papers.abstract: Motor recovery after stroke depends on neuroplasticity-driven reorganisation of surviving cortical circuits. A growing body of evidence implicates sleep as an active consolidator of motor memories acquired during rehabilitation. Yet stroke disrupts the very sleep architecture required for this process, and current clinical practice schedules rehabilitation without regard for its temporal proximity to sleep. This review synthesizes the mechanistic, preclinical, and emerging clinical evidence underlying the rehabilitation timing hypothesis. Sleep spindles, nested within slow oscillations during NREM sleep, are a principal electrophysiological substrate for motor memory consolidation, and emerging evidence implicates cerebellar-cortical dynamics during spindles. Stroke disrupts this oscillatory coupling through lesion-related alterations in thalamocortical circuitry, GABAergic signalling, and interhemispheric synchrony. Preclinical studies demonstrate that optogenetically-enhanced slow waves during sleep accelerate motor recovery, while pharmacological GABA modulation restores consolidation-promoting oscillations. Chronobiological evidence from healthy adults and older populations suggests that evening training followed by nocturnal sleep may produce superior long-term motor retention compared with morning training. The rehabilitation timing hypothesis is plausible and clinically testable, but direct evidence in stroke populations is currently lacking. Scheduling motor therapy close to sleep is a low-cost strategy that warrants formal evaluation as a means of enhancing stroke recovery. Formal clinical trials testing therapy timing as an independent variable are urgently needed.

papers.title: Sex differences in associations between sleep architecture and CBC-derived immune cell indices in MDD with comorbid insomnia.
papers.abstract: Insomnia symptoms and alterations in sleep architecture are core pathophysiological features of Major Depressive Disorder (MDD). While sex differences in MDD prevalence and symptomatology are well documented, the specific interplay between sleep architecture and complete blood count (CBC)-derived immune cell indices, metabolic markers, and thyroid-related parameters remains under-characterized with respect to sex. This study included 126 patients with MDD and comorbid insomnia (43 males, 83 females). All participants underwent overnight polysomnography (PSG) and fasting blood biochemical analysis. Sex-specific associations between objective sleep parameters and peripheral biomarkers were analyzed using age-adjusted partial Spearman correlation and multiple linear regression models with interaction terms. Female patients had longer REM sleep latency and N2 sleep duration, whereas male patients had a higher apnea-hypopnea index. Females had higher HDL-C levels, while males had higher monocyte counts. In age-adjusted FDR-corrected correlation analyses, significant associations involving CBC-derived immune cell counts were observed primarily in male patients, where lymphocyte count was associated with TST, REM sleep duration, N1%, and N2 sleep duration; no significant CBC-derived immune cell count correlations remained in female patients. In multivariable interaction analyses with FDR correction, sex × lymphocyte interaction terms remained significant for TMA, REM sleep duration, and REM sleep duration relative to TST. These findings suggest that sex may shape both the subjective-objective expression of sleep disturbance and lymphocyte-related sleep regulation in patients with MDD and comorbid insomnia. The pattern of poorer subjective sleep quality despite relatively favorable selected PSG characteristics in females, together with sex-dependent lymphocyte associations involving REM sleep and arousal measures, warrants further validation in larger longitudinal studies. Not applicable.

papers.title: Circadian-melatonin signaling in general anesthesia: molecular mechanisms and perioperative implications.
papers.abstract: Anesthesia and surgery are delivered to a temporally organized organism whose physiology is governed by the suprachiasmatic nucleus, peripheral molecular clocks, and pineal melatonin signaling. This review synthesizes mechanistic, preclinical, and clinical evidence on how anesthetic agents, surgical stress, and the perioperative environment interact with circadian and melatonergic signaling, and on whether that interaction can be targeted therapeutically. In rodent and cellular studies, volatile and intravenous anesthetics alter clock function in an agent- and phase-dependent manner; proposed mechanisms include GABAergic and glutamatergic modulation of entrainment, transcriptional and chromatin-level repression of CLOCK-BMAL1/PER-CRY signaling, and metabolic coupling through CaMK-CREB, AMPK, SIRT1, and GSK-3β. These mechanisms have not been confirmed in humans. In patients, these effects are inseparable from surgical injury, opioids, fasting, inflammation, and disrupted light-dark exposure, all of which suppress melatonin amplitude, delay its onset, and promote internal desynchrony. Melatonin signals through MT1 and MT2 receptors to produce chronobiotic, anxiolytic, and antinociceptive effects, whereas the mitochondrial, redox, and anti-inflammatory actions, described almost exclusively in animal and cellular models, require substantially higher exposures and have not been demonstrated in surgical patients; the two arms are pharmacologically distinct and should not be pooled. Clinically, preoperative anxiolysis with melatonin in adults is the most consistently supported indication, whereas evidence for postoperative sleep, analgesia, delirium prevention, and organ protection remains heterogeneous and of low certainty. Most trials have used fixed clock-time dosing without measuring internal circadian phase or achieved plasma exposure, so null results cannot distinguish an ineffective mechanism from an inadequate intervention. The circadian-melatonin axis remains a plausible perioperative target, but clinical translation requires phase-aware, exposure-informed, and adequately powered trials.

papers.title: Validation of the Telephone MoCA in iRBD and Parkinson's Disease with Conversion to the Standard MoCA.
papers.abstract: Telephone-based cognitive assessment may improve follow-up when face-to-face testing is impractical. The Telephone Montreal Cognitive Assessment (T-MoCA) omits visually dependent items from the standard MoCA, but its validity in isolated REM sleep behavior disorder (iRBD) and Parkinson's disease (PD), remains uncertain. To assess agreement between the T-MoCA and face-to-face MoCA-22 in iRBD and PD, and derive and externally validate a MoCA-22 to MoCA-30 conversion. In the Oxford Parkinson's Disease Centre (OPDC) Discovery Cohort, 137 participants (38 controls, 47 iRBD, 52 PD) completed T-MoCA and MoCA-22 assessments. Agreement was evaluated using Lin's concordance correlation coefficient, Bland-Altman analysis, and equivalence testing with ±1-point bounds. Equipercentile equating with log-linear smoothing was used to derive a MoCA-22 to MoCA-30 conversion using Discovery data (3561 tests), with validation in Tracking Parkinson's (5767 tests) and Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (5047 tests). T-MoCA and face-to-face MoCA-22 scores were statistically equivalent, with minimal bias; 83.3% of scores differed by ≤1 point. However, concordance between test formats was moderate (Lin's CCC = 0.58). Across 14,375 MoCA assessments, equipercentile equating outperformed proportional scaling in development and validation cohorts. Propagating T-MoCA-MoCA-22 variability resulted in wider prediction intervals for T-MoCA-derived MoCA-30 estimates, indicating individual-level uncertainty, with intervals estimable only for T-MoCA scores ≥17 due to sparse data. At group level, T-MoCA is a valid remote measure of non-visual MoCA domains in iRBD and PD. The equating function supports cohort-level harmonization of MoCA-22 and MoCA-30 scores, while individual T-MoCA-derived MoCA-30 estimates should be interpreted with caution.

papers.title: Vulnerability of the Brainstem-Cerebellar Respiratory Network in Extreme Prematurity.
papers.abstract: Survival of extremely preterm infants has significantly improved over the past decades, shifting critical stages of respiratory and brain development into the extrauterine environment. This transition exposes the vulnerable preterm infant to abrupt changes in oxygen tension, intermittent hypoxemia, inflammation, and oxidative stress, which contribute to maldevelopment of the structure and function of immature organs, including the brain and brainstem, with short- and long-term adverse consequences. This review examines how adverse intrauterine and extrauterine exposures during critical developmental periods in extremely low gestational age neonates (ELGANs) born <28 weeks of gestation disrupt the structure and function of key components of the central respiratory network, supporting epidemiological evidence that premature infants have a substantially increased risk of sudden unexpected infant death (SUID) during the first year of life and sleep disordered breathing across the lifespan. ELGANs are born during a period of rapid brainstem and cerebellar development, increasing the vulnerability of these regions to oxidative and inflammatory injury that can cause direct tissue damage and dysmaturation. The medullary serotonergic network and cerebellar fastigial nucleus regulate cardiorespiratory responses at rest and during progressive hypoxia and hypercapnia. We propose that adverse intrauterine and extrauterine exposures during critical developmental windows damage the macro- and microstructures, neurochemistry of these regions, impair protective respiratory responses, and mechanistically contribute to the two- to threefold higher risk of SUID in ELGANs than in term infants. We review fetal neuroprotective responses to hypoxia; the mechanisms and vulnerability of brain injury in ELGANs; the development and intrinsic hypoxic chemosensitivity of central respiratory control; and brainstem and cerebellar dysmaturation. Together, this framework provides a biological basis linking extreme prematurity to impaired ventilatory control, disordered breathing, and increased vulnerability to sudden death during infancy and beyond.

papers.title: A multi-session simultaneous EEG-fMRI dataset with repeated experience sampling
papers.abstract: The integration of electroencephalography (EEG) and functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) can be used to characterize temporal and spatial components of neural activity during unfolding mental experience. Here we introduce a multi-session simultaneous EEG-fMRI dataset with measures of continuous behavior and spontaneous mental experience. Data components, organized in Brain Imaging Dataset Structure (BIDS) format, include fMRI, EEG with carbon wire loop sensors for artifact removal, continuous performance task responses, experience sampling ratings, and mental health surveys, from 24 healthy adults. Tasks included the gradual-onset continuous performance task and resting state with intermittent experience sampling of 13 unique thought dimensions (36 repetitions, including 468 total ratings, per participant). The same protocol was completed on two different days, yielding approximately 1.33 hours of simultaneous EEG-fMRI data per individual. The dataset may be used to explore the behavioral and experiential relevance of brain activity during the wakeful resting state. The dataset also provides a means to study the reliability of relationships between fMRI and EEG features across sessions within individuals.

The dataset supports study of brain activity during wakeful rest and cross-session reliability of EEG-fMRI relationships.

papers.title: Improved Sleep and Clinical Outcomes Following a Single-Session Intervention among Adolescents with Borderline Personality Disorder Features
papers.abstract: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is a serious mental illness that often emerges in adolescence. Although efficacious treatments have been developed, they are often lengthy, expensive, inaccessible, and require specialized training to deliver. Optimizing BPD prevention and early treatment is an important public health priority. Youth also collected at-home ambulatory electroencephalogram (EEG) recordings before undergoing the treatment informed by the Transdiagnostic Sleep and Circadian Intervention. papers.title: Traditional Chinese medicine-related interventions and the cGAS-STING axis in neuroinflammation: disease contexts and mechanisms of action.
papers.abstract: Research on traditional Chinese medicine (TCM)-related interventions has shifted from overall phenotypic effects to defined neuroimmune targets. The cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) axis connects cytosolic DNA sensing with host defense and sterile inflammatory injury, but the functional direction of this pathway changes with disease context. This review organizes preclinical findings by pathological setting and site of action. It examines herbal formulas and natural compounds, followed by acupuncture, electroacupuncture, and related delivery systems. Several sterile injury models associate benefit with reduced pathway-related inflammation. Acute sleep deprivation provides an example of protection accompanying restored STING signaling. Early herpes simplex virus infection follows a different pattern: restoration of suppressed antiviral signaling improves host defense. In acute postoperative pain and cancer-induced bone pain models, increased STING-IFN-I signaling accompanies electroacupuncture-induced analgesia. Some interventions reduce mitochondrial DNA stimulation. Others act on cGAS or STING, with separate studies targeting STING trafficking. Downstream inflammatory and cell-death responses form the final level. Mechanistic attribution is strongest when genetic or pharmacological perturbation links pathway change to functional outcome; direct binding has been demonstrated for a small group of compounds. These findings support a context-sensitive framework for interpreting modulation direction that requires validation within individual disease models. Clinical translation will depend on reproducible formulation composition, effective brain exposure, and safety.

papers.title: Mental replay rescales the subjective duration of past events via alpha and theta oscillations
papers.abstract: Human memory recall is flexible in time, allowing past events to be mentally replayed at variable speeds. However, it remains unclear whether temporally rescaled replay distorts the perceived duration of remembered events, and whether such distortion is tied to changes in the retrieved content. Here we instructed participants to mentally replay previously encoded naturalistic videos at compressed, expanded, or self-paced (free) speeds while recording scalp electroencephalography (EEG). Replaying an event at an expanded pace lengthened participants' subsequent judgments of its original duration relative to free and compressed replay, and the longer an event had been replayed, the longer it was judged to have lasted. Crucially, recalled memory content was unaffected, with gist accuracy and recalled detail comparable across speed conditions. During replay, alpha and theta power were reduced under compression, and both interacted with the speed instruction in predicting reported duration. Specifically, alpha power exhibited a stronger positive relationship with duration judgments under compressed replay than under free or expanded replay. Conversely, the relationship between theta power and reported duration was significantly more positive under expanded replay than under free or compressed replay. Neural pattern similarity between instructed and later spontaneous replay varied with replay speed, yet this reinstatement neither predicted reported duration nor mediated the oscillatory effects. These findings suggest that remembered duration is not read out from the amount of content retrieved but reconstructed at retrieval through oscillatory dynamics, decoupling the subjective scaling of time from the content of memory.

papers.title: Sleep deprivation compromises sperm quality and early embryo development by disrupting folate metabolism and DNA repair.
papers.abstract: Sleep deprivation (SD), a prevalent modern lifestyle issue, has been associated with impaired male reproductive function, yet the underlying molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. In a mouse model, sustained SD triggered germ cell apoptosis, reduced sperm motility, and increased morphological abnormalities. Furthermore, SD compromised sperm fertilization capacity and impaired preimplantation embryo development. Proteomic analysis identified SLC46A1, a proton-coupled folate transporter, as the only consistently downregulated protein in both testicular tissue and sperm. Furthermore, the expression of methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR), a key enzyme in folate metabolism, was also markedly decreased, accompanied by reduced levels of core DNA repair proteins (RAD51 and TOPBP1). Notably, folate supplementation prior to and during SD partially restored the expression of MTHFR, RAD51, and TOPBP1, suggesting that enhanced folate availability can counteract some of the molecular alterations induced by SD. Collectively, our findings suggest a mechanistic link whereby SD disrupts folate transport and metabolism, potentially compromising DNA repair in sperm and thereby impairing sperm quality and embryonic development. This suggests that targeting folate metabolism may offer a therapeutic strategy to mitigate SD-associated male infertility.

papers.title: Seasonal Variation in Mood and Associated Patterns of Sleep, Activity, Circadian Rhythms and Light.
papers.abstract: The mechanisms underlying seasonal mood variation are incompletely characterised. Each observation included a clinical assessment paired with ≥5 valid days of wrist actigraphy. Season was modelled using sine-cosine functions of day-of-year. Sleep, activity and circadian features were reduced using joint and individual variation explained (JIVE). Light exposure features were reduced using principal component analysis (PCA) applied to light regularity, timing and exposure interval across 7 illuminance thresholds. Linear mixed-effects models tested seasonal effects on clinical outcomes; indirect associations for 12 candidate JIVE/PCA variables were estimated by cluster bootstrap. Depressive symptoms (β = -0.67, P = .023) and negative symptoms (β = -0.17, P = .041) peaked in winter, whereas manic symptoms peaked in autumn (β = 0.24, P = .019). Winter increases in negative symptoms were associated with an 'extended sleep with phase-delayed activity' profile (indirect β = -0.015, P < .002) and a 'constrained pattern of moderate-to-bright indoor light exposure' profile (indirect β = -0.038, P = .002), reflecting high day-to-day consistency with a narrow daily exposure window. The light association persisted after adjustment for time spent above the light threshold, which itself was not associated with symptoms. Winter increases in depressive symptoms were associated with lower overall physical activity levels (indirect β = -0.009, P = .040). No indirect associations were identified for manic symptoms. In this transdiagnostic youth sample, seasonal variation in mood was modest but was accompanied by differences in how personal light exposure was arranged across the day, not only in how much light was received and in daily activity patterns. papers.title: EEG-Based Cognitive Overload-Driven Adaptive Training for Enhancing Performance Under Simulated High-Stress Space Operation Tasks.
papers.abstract: Given the potential for highly complex and high-risk space operation tasks to induce cognitive overload in operators, effective training is crucial for maintaining mission performance and safety. To address this limitation, this study proposes an EEG-based cognitive overload-driven adaptive training method that integrates hybrid feature selection, Normalized Fast Dynamic Time Warping (NFDTW)-based feature alignment and a shared knowledge layer to improve online cognitive overload detection under nonstationary conditions. A dual-factor task regulation strategy combining task performance and cognitive overload states is further developed to adjust task difficulty based on these two factors. The results showed that the proposed detection method achieved online detection accuracies of 92.07% and 84.67% on the two datasets, respectively, with maximum relative improvements of 7.74% and 8.34% over the comparison methods. The adaptive training strategy was further evaluated in a VR-based robotic arm docking task involving three groups: fixed, control, and adaptive. Mixed-design ANOVA showed that the adaptive group exhibited significant improvements in task performance and SAS as well as more favorable changes in EEG features. Bonferroni-adjusted post hoc comparisons further revealed significant group differences ([Formula: see text]). papers.title: EEG Feature-level integration for robust command generation in SSVEP-based brain-computer interfaces.
papers.abstract: Steady-state visual evoked potential (SSVEP)-based brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have been widely studied for efficient command generation via spatiotemporal information integration and advanced stimulation paradigms. However, users may intentionally or unintentionally suppress SSVEP responses, leading to the SSVEP Blocking Response (SSVEP-BR). This phenomenon, characterized by attenuation or disappearance of SSVEP, has been largely overlooked despite its potential for command generation without additional stimuli. This study aimed to exploit SSVEP-BR to enhance command generation under limited visual stimulation. A novel detection method was proposed based on alpha rhythm sensitivity during transitions between SSVEP and SSVEP-BR states. An EEG feature-level integration strategy was further developed to integrate correlation and alpha rhythm features, enabling effective characterization of their temporal evolution. An asynchronous BCI system was implemented for real-time robotic arm control. Experiments on 11 offline subjects demonstrated that the proposed method improved SSVEP-BR detection performance. Compared with the previous SSVEP-BR detection framework, average improvements of 17.11%, 8.50%, and 5.44% were achieved in precision, recall, and specificity, respectively. Furthermore, an online robotic grasping experiment was conducted with 5 subjects, where the proposed asynchronous BCI system achieved 8-command generation using two stimulation frequencies. Unlike prior studies focusing on algorithmic optimization or stimulation design, this work introduced SSVEP-BR as an additional controllable neural response and demonstrated its effectiveness in improving command generation without increasing stimulus complexity. papers.title: Outcome-Blind EEG Microstate Topography After Cardiac Arrest: Spatial Expression of a Lateralized Microstate and Association with Neurological Outcome.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is central to neurological assessment after cardiac arrest, yet conventional approaches predominantly characterize amplitude, frequency content, continuity, suppression, reactivity, or predefined pathological patterns. EEG microstates provide a complementary framework by describing quasi-stable configurations of the global scalp electric field. We investigated whether an outcome-blind microstate decomposition of EEG from comatose survivors of cardiac arrest identifies reproducible spatial states associated with neurological outcome. We performed a secondary analysis of the multicenter I-CARE/PhysioNet database. Following prespecified EEG screening requiring continuous 19-channel recordings of at least 300 s, 567 subjects were included (34 excluded at preflight). Microstate reconstruction was performed outcome-blind using a fixed 300-s continuous baseline analysis window, GFP-peak sampling capped at 500 peaks per patient, and polarity-invariant clustering across K = 2-10. After model-order evaluation, the K = 4 solution was frozen and backfitted at the patient level. Associations between microstate metrics and neurological outcome were evaluated using unadjusted, multivariable, dose-response, ROC discrimination, and extensive resampling analyses. The primary outcome analysis included 567 patients: 209 with favorable (CPC 1-2) and 358 with unfavorable (CPC 3-5) neurological outcomes. M2 global explained variance (GEV) was higher in patients with favorable outcome (median 0.0852 vs. 0.0564; rank-biserial correlation = 0.185; p = 0.000243; false-discovery-rate [FDR]-adjusted p = 0.000568 within the four-state GEV family). M2 GEV was inversely associated with CPC severity (Spearman rho = -0.144; p = 0.000583; FDR-adjusted p = 0.001419). Standalone ROC analysis yielded an AUC of 0.59 (95% CI 0.54-0.64). After adjustment for age, sex, and shockable rhythm in the extended cohort without return-of-spontaneous-circulation (ROSC) time (N = 535), each 1-SD increase in M2 GEV was associated with greater odds of favorable outcome (OR 1.30, 95% CI 1.07-1.58; p = 0.0092). By contrast, M2 coverage, mean duration, and occurrence were not significantly associated with outcome after multiplicity correction. An outcome-blind decomposition of EEG after cardiac arrest identified a frozen microstate, M2, whose GEV was reproducibly associated with neurological outcome. The prognostic information associated with M2 was related primarily to the degree to which this spatial configuration explained the global EEG field rather than to its conventional temporal parameters. papers.title: Personal nighttime indoor temperature and sleep characteristics in adults with type 2 diabetes.
papers.abstract: To examine whether personal nighttime indoor temperature is associated with actigraphy-derived sleep outcomes among community-dwelling adults with type 2 diabetes. We analyzed repeated-night data from 108 adults with type 2 diabetes, contributing 1307 paired sleep-temperature nights. Personal nighttime indoor temperature was measured with temperature loggers and averaged across each participant-specific nocturnal sleep episode. Sleep outcomes included sleep efficiency, wake after sleep onset, total sleep time, and number of awakenings. Linear mixed-effects models examined within-person and between-person temperature-sleep associations. Generalized additive mixed models evaluated nonlinearity. Models were adjusted for sociodemographic, clinical, and seasonal covariates. Personal nighttime indoor temperature and sleep outcomes varied across nights, with both showing seasonal patterns. In adjusted linear mixed-effects models, warmer-than-usual nights were associated with higher sleep efficiency and fewer awakenings, whereas between-person average temperature was not associated with any sleep outcomes. Model-predicted sleep outcomes remained largely unchanged across moderate nighttime indoor temperatures. Findings suggest that nighttime indoor temperature may be relevant to sleep health promotion and diabetes-related sleep counseling, particularly for adults reporting poor sleep or limited control over indoor temperature.

papers.title: The moderating role of anger rumination and self-control in the day-to-day associations between irritability and sleep in male adolescents: An exploratory experience sampling method study.

papers.title: Depth-adaptive suppression of subject-dependent interference for robust cross-subject EEG emotion recognition.

Selective depth-aware suppression provides a practical and interpretable strategy for robust EEG-based affective brain-computer interfaces.

papers.title: E-MDD: an evidence-guided explainable framework for EEG-based depression recognition.

Twenty scenarios were developed across type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU), representing matched mild and moderate presentations of depression and anxiety together with condition-specific distress related to diabetes self-management and CSU-related flare uncertainty. Each scenario was independently submitted to all three systems in two testing rounds, yielding 120 responses. Blinded raters assessed overall psychological support appropriateness, recognition and emotional support, chronic-illness contextualization, psychological support and referral, psychosomatic balance and safety, and major clinical or safety errors. Repeated testing assessed response consistency. Overall psychological support appropriateness differed across systems (P = 0.002), with 90.0% of ChatGPT, 75.0% of Gemini, and 55.0% of Doubao responses meeting the prespecified appropriateness threshold. Recognition and emotional support was consistently strong across systems, whereas greater differences emerged in chronic-illness contextualization (P = 0.001), psychological support and referral (P = 0.002), and psychosomatic balance and safety (P<0.001). All responses to mild presentations were classified as psychologically appropriate, compared with 58.3% of responses to moderate presentations, indicating that performance became less reliable when digital support required stronger escalation toward professional assessment. Contextualization was also less consistent in CSU, particularly when responses needed to incorporate flare unpredictability, pruritus, sleep disruption, and illness uncertainty. Major clinical or safety errors occurred in 0%, 10.0%, and 15.0% of first-round ChatGPT, Gemini, and Doubao responses, respectively. Test-retest consistency was moderate and varied between systems. General-purpose AI chatbots show potential as accessible, self-guided digital mental health resources for people living with chronic conditions, particularly for recognizing distress and providing initial supportive guidance. Their current limitations emerge when effective support requires disease-specific contextualization, balanced interpretation of psychological and somatic factors, or escalation as symptoms become more severe. These findings identify important boundaries for the use of conversational AI in chronic-illness mental health care and suggest that implementation should emphasize context-sensitive guidance, severity-responsive referral, and clear integration with rather than substitution for professional care.

papers.title: Autonomy satisfaction and bedtime procrastination among generation Z university students: The serial mediating roles of general self-efficacy and AI dependence.
papers.abstract: With the rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education, university students' daily behaviors are increasingly shaped by technology use. Bedtime procrastination has emerged as a common self-regulation problem among Generation Z students. However, the psychological mechanisms linking environmental resources and technology-related behaviors to sleep outcomes remain insufficiently understood. This study examined the associations between autonomy satisfaction and bedtime procrastination and the mediating roles of general self-efficacy and AI dependence. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 717 Chinese university students using cluster sampling. Standardized self-report measures assessed autonomy satisfaction, general self-efficacy, AI dependence, and bedtime procrastination. Data were analyzed using SPSS 26.0 and Mplus 8.0. Structural equation modeling and bias-corrected bootstrap (5000 resamples) were employed to test direct and indirect effects. Autonomy satisfaction was positively associated with general self-efficacy and negatively associated with AI dependence and bedtime procrastination. General self-efficacy was negatively associated with both AI dependence and bedtime procrastination, while AI dependence was positively associated with bedtime procrastination. Mediation analysis revealed that both general self-efficacy and AI dependence served as significant mediators, with AI dependence accounting for a larger proportion of the indirect effect. A significant serial mediation pathway was also observed. The findings suggest that autonomy satisfaction was associated with bedtime procrastination through both cognitive and behavioral mechanisms. AI dependence plays a particularly important role as a proximal behavioral pathway. These results highlight the need to promote balanced AI use and strengthen students' self-regulation in technology-rich learning environments.

papers.title: The Moderating Effect of Sleep Duration on the Association Between Chronic Disease and Health-Related Quality of Life in Middle-Aged Women.
papers.abstract: This cross-sectional secondary data analysis aimed to examine the association between the number of chronic diseases and health-related quality of life (HRQOL) in middle-aged women and to determine whether sleep duration moderated this association. Data from 3062 women aged 46-70 years were obtained from the 2019 and 2021 Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Surveys. Complex-samples t-tests, analysis of variance, and multiple regression analyses were conducted. A significant moderating effect of sleep duration was observed for the > 9 h/day group compared with the > 6-7 h/day reference group (p = 0.016), with a stronger negative association between the number of chronic diseases and HRQOL in this group. Participants in the > 6-7 h/day and > 7-8 h/day groups reported significantly higher HRQOL than those sleeping ≤ 5, > 8-9, and > 9 h/day (p < 0.001), and a greater number of chronic diseases was associated with lower HRQOL (p < 0.001). These findings suggest that sleep duration, particularly sleep duration of more than 9 h, may be considered when evaluating the association between the number of chronic diseases and HRQOL among middle-aged women.

papers.title: Network analysis of frailty, sleep quality, and life satisfaction in older patients: a cross-sectional study stratified by chronic disease burden.
papers.abstract: Multimorbidity and chronic disease burden are common among older patients and are closely associated with frailty, poor sleep, and reduced subjective well-being. However, total-score-based analyses may obscure item-level interactions across health domains. This study examined the network structure of frailty, sleep quality, and life satisfaction in older patients and explored whether association patterns varied across chronic disease burden levels. This cross-sectional study included 1,107 older patients. Multimorbidity was defined as the presence of two or more chronic diseases. Frailty, sleep quality, and life satisfaction were assessed using the Fatigue, Resistance, Ambulation, Illnesses, and Loss of Weight (FRAIL) scale, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and Satisfaction With Life Scale (SWLS), respectively. A regularized partial correlation network was estimated using the graphical least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) with extended Bayesian information criterion (EBIC) model selection (EBICglasso), with scale items or components as nodes. Strength, expected influence, and bridge centrality were calculated. Stratified analyses were conducted by number of chronic diseases, and bootstrap procedures were used to assess network accuracy and stability. Multimorbidity was present in 1,078 participants (97.4%), and the median number of chronic diseases was 5 (IQR, 3-6). Network analysis showed that SWLS-related nodes had relatively high strength and bridge strength, indicating relatively high statistical connectivity within the overall network and across communities. Sleep-related nodes, particularly sleep latency, use of sleeping medication, and daytime dysfunction, were prominent in signed centrality indices. Frailty nodes were mainly connected to SWLS nodes through negative edges. The SWLS community showed dense internal connections, whereas frailty and sleep quality were linked to life satisfaction primarily through negative cross-community edges. In descriptive stratified analyses, negative cross-community connections appeared more pronounced in the group with ≥ 5 chronic diseases. Because the cutoff was data-driven and no formal network comparison test was performed, the apparent between-group differences should be interpreted as descriptive and exploratory rather than statistically confirmed. Network stability analyses indicated acceptable stability. Among older patients, life satisfaction-related nodes showed relatively high overall connectivity, while several sleep-related nodes showed notable statistical associations within the estimated network. Given the high prevalence of multimorbidity in this sample, multidisciplinary assessment and health management should consider the interrelations among sleep problems, frailty, and life satisfaction in the context of chronic disease burden. Network analysis may provide exploratory evidence on cross-domain associations in complex health problems among older patients, but apparent differences across chronic disease burden groups require confirmation using formal network comparison tests and longitudinal designs.

papers.title: EEG decodability of facial expressions and their stereoscopic depth cues in immersive virtual reality
papers.abstract: Face perception typically occurs in three-dimensional space, where stereoscopic depth cues enrich the perception of facial features. Yet, most neurophysiological research on face processing relies on two-dimensional displays, potentially overlooking the role of stereoscopic depth information. Here, we combine immersive virtual reality (VR), electroencephalography (EEG), and eye tracking to examine the neural representation of faces under controlled manipulations of stereoscopic depth. Thirty-four participants viewed computer-generated faces with neutral, happy, angry, and surprised expressions in frontal view under monoscopic and stereoscopic viewing conditions. Using time-resolved multivariate decoding, we show that EEG signals in immersive VR conditions can reliably differentiate facial expressions. Stereoscopic depth cues elicited a distinct and decodable neural signature, confirming the sensitivity of our approach to depth-related processing. Yet, expression decoding remained robust across depth conditions, indicating that under controlled frontal viewing, the neural representation of behaviorally distinguishable facial expressions is invariant to binocular depth cues. Eye tracking showed that expression-related gaze patterns contained comparable information but did not account for neural representations, while depth information was absent in gaze patterns--consistent with dissociable representational processes. Our findings demonstrate the feasibility of EEG-based neural decoding in fully immersive VR as a tool for investigating face perception in naturalistic settings and provide new evidence for the stability of expression representations across depth variations in three-dimensional viewing conditions.

papers.title: Case Report: Smith-Magenis syndrome with bilateral high-grade vesicoureteral reflux, hypothyroidism, and seizure in infancy.
papers.abstract: Smith-Magenis syndrome (SMS) is a rare neurodevelopmental and multisystem disorder caused mainly by 17p11.2 deletions involving RAI1. Because the characteristic behavioral and sleep phenotype may not yet be apparent, diagnosis in infancy can be challenging. We report a 9-month-old boy with recurrent febrile urinary tract infection, bilateral hydronephrosis with ureteral dilatation, hypothyroidism, global developmental delay, hypotonia, brachydactyly, dysmorphic features, phimosis, and short penis. Voiding cystourethrography demonstrated bilateral grade IV vesicoureteral reflux (VUR). Renal scintigraphy showed focal right renal cortical defects; DTPA effective renal plasma flow was 180.33 mL/min in the left kidney and 133.77 mL/min in the right kidney, corresponding to split function of 57.4% and 42.6%. Trio whole-exome sequencing with copy-number-variant analysis identified a de novo 3.63-Mb deletion at 17p11.2 encompassing RAI1, confirming SMS; a maternally inherited heterozygous DUOX2 likely pathogenic variant was also detected, but its contribution to hypothyroidism remains unproven. Infection improved with antibiotics, levothyroxine was resumed, and amoxicillin/clavulanate prophylaxis was initiated. Surgery for phimosis was postponed after an afebrile sleep-related seizure. Follow-up showed improved renal indices, no recurrent urinary tract infection, normalized thyroid function, and no definite abnormality on video-electroencephalography, although developmental delay persisted and brief seizure-like ocular events remained under evaluation. This case shows that high-grade bilateral VUR with recurrent infection and a syndromic neurodevelopmental phenotype can be an early presentation of SMS and warrants copy-number analysis, renal protection, and coordinated endocrine, neurologic, developmental, and urologic follow-up.

papers.title: Patient-Reported Outcomes with High-Volume Hemodiafiltration Versus High-Flux Hemodialysis Across Clinical Subgroups: Results from the CONVINCE Trial.
papers.abstract: High-volume hemodiafiltration (HDF) improves survival and attenuates decline in selected patient-reported outcome (PRO) domains versus high-flux hemodialysis (HD). Whether benefits differ across clinically relevant subgroups remains uncertain. We conducted a prespecified subgroup analysis of the multicenter CONVINCE randomized controlled trial comparing high-volume post-dilution HDF (≥23 L/session) with high-flux HD in adults receiving maintenance dialysis. Eight PROMIS domains were assessed quarterly over a median follow-up of 30 months. Linear mixed-effects models evaluated longitudinal PRO changes and treatment-by-subgroup interactions by prespecified baseline characteristics: age, sex, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, dialysis vintage, vascular access type, and residual urine volume. Joint-model sensitivity analyses of all eight longitudinal PROMIS trajectories and time to death assessed informative dropout due to death. Of 1360 randomized participants, 1211 with baseline and follow-up PRO assessments were included. PRO treatment effects were broadly consistent across prespecified clinical subgroups, without evidence of clinically meaningful heterogeneity. Models adjusted for baseline sociodemographic and clinical characteristics showed nominal treatment-by-subgroup interactions for dialysis vintage and physical function (P = 0.03), age and pain interference (P = 0.02), and dialysis vintage and sleep disturbance (P = 0.04). Joint-model sensitivity analyses accounting for informative dropout due to mortality reproduced the first two interactions and identified nominal interactions for vascular access type and sleep disturbance (P = 0.03) and cardiovascular disease status and cognitive function (P = 0.05). Interactions were modest in magnitude, exploratory, unadjusted for multiple comparisons, and not consistently observed across related PROMIS domains. This prespecified exploratory subgroup analysis found no convincing evidence of clinically meaningful treatment-effect heterogeneity across baseline characteristics examined. Nominal interactions were unadjusted for multiple comparisons and should be regarded as hypothesis-generating. Findings should not guide selection or exclusion of patients for high-volume HDF based on patient-reported outcomes.

papers.title: Association between lactic dehydrogenase-to-albumin ratio and all-cause mortality in critical obstructive sleep apnea patients: a retrospective cohort study from the MIMIC-IV database.
papers.abstract: Our study endeavors to elucidate the link of the lactic dehydrogenase-to-albumin ratio (LDAR) to all-cause mortality (ACM) among the critically ill obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) population. A retrospective observational cohort study was performed leveraging the MIMIC-IV 3.1 data. This study encompassed adult OSA patients first entering the intensive care unit (ICU). Patients were stratified into quartiles by LDAR. The primary outcomes were ACM at 30, 90, 180 days, and one year after ICU entry. ACM across LDAR quartiles was compared via the Kaplan-Meier (KM) survival analysis. The relation of LDAR to ACM was examined utilizing multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression and restricted cubic spline (RCS) models. The consistency and robustness of our findings were rated through subgroup, interaction, and sensitivity analyses. One thousand one hundred eighteen critically ill OSA patients were encompassed. 749 (66.99%) were male, with a median age of 66. The 30-day, 90-day, 180-day, and one-year ACM rates were 14.58%, 19.59%, 22.00%, and 26.74%. KM curves demonstrated significantly higher mortality rates across increasing LDAR quartiles (log-rank P < 0.001). After possible confounders were adjusted, LDAR was independently related to elevated 90-day ACM risk (HR, 1.318; 95%CI, 1.142-1.520) as a continuous variable. In contrast to the lowest LDAR quartile, the highest quartile displayed a 139.8% greater likelihood of 90-day ACM (HR, 2.398; 95%CI, 1.512-3.803; Ptrend < 0.001). Similar relations were noted for 30-day, 180-day, and one-year ACM. RCS analysis revealed a positive linear relation of LDAR to death at all time points (Pnonlinear > 0.05). Subgroup and interaction analyses revealed insignificant effect modification, confirming the robustness of the association across various clinical strata. Among the critically ill OSA population, elevated LDAR is independently and linearly related to elevated ACM risk in short-term and long-term mortality. The foregoing findings suggest LDAR as a valuable prognostic biomarker for risk classification and clinical management among this high-risk population.

papers.title: A systematic review of economic evaluations of strategies to diagnose obstructive sleep apnoea in adults.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) is a chronic condition characterised by recurrent episodes of apnoea and hypopnoea. People with untreated OSA are at increased risk of excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS), functional impairment and developing cardiovascular conditions, metabolic and neurocognitive diseases. EDS is a key determinant of quality of life (QoL) and is associated with increased healthcare utilisation and accident risk. Untreated OSA can also lead to impaired work productivity, reduced health-related quality of life (HRQoL) and life expectancy, which contribute to the UK economic burden. To review and critically appraise all published economic evaluations that assessed the cost-effectiveness of devices and strategies to diagnose and manage people with moderate-to-severe OSA. This systematic review was conducted following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews guidelines and registered in the Prospective Register of Ongoing Systematic Reviews (CRD42024535732). We searched electronic databases up to March 2025. Two reviewers undertook screening, data extraction and quality appraisal using recognised reporting quality and methodological quality appraisal tools. The findings were summarised and discussed narratively. Twenty-nine studies were included. Fifteen studies included an economic evaluation alongside a clinical trial and 14 studies were model-based economic analyses. Although many analyses were methodologically sound in their overall approach, there were concerns regarding choice of time horizon, selection of health states, undertaking pre-model analyses and long-term adherence and efficacy of continuous positive airway pressure treatment (CPAP). Substantial methodological heterogeneity was identified across studies, including variation in diagnostic thresholds and scoring criteria used, model structures and assumptions regarding treatment adherence. Only four of twenty-nine included studies used home respiratory polygraphy (HRP) as a comparator, limiting the direct applicability of much of the evidence to the UK setting. Past economic analyses offer insight into the methods used to assess the cost-effectiveness of strategies to diagnose OSA. These economic analyses are a useful framework to build on, but clear gaps exist in the clinical and economic evidence. Future economic evaluations should prioritise contemporary diagnostic pathways and technologies, use consistent diagnostic definitions, and incorporate more realistic modelling of long-term treatment adherence and benefit. Until such information becomes available, the true cost-effectiveness of these strategies remains unknown.

papers.title: "It Just Puts You Out!" Tranq Sleep, Sensory Discernment, and the Experience of Consuming Xylazine-Adulterated Fentanyl in Rural North Carolina
papers.abstract: Background: Xylazine, a veterinary sedative not approved for human use, has emerged as a consequential adulterant in the U.S. illicit fentanyl supply. Although a growing body of qualitative research has documented the experiences of fentanyl consumers exposed to tranq in large Northeastern cities, little is known about how xylazine is experienced in rural or Southern regions where the evolution of the illicit drug supply often lags behind its urban equivalents. This study examines how fentanyl consumers in west-central North Carolina detect, comprehend and respond to the widespread adulteration of fentanyl markets with xylazine. Methods: Between September and December of 2025, a seasoned interviewer conducted 25 in-depth, semi-structured qualitative interviews with fentanyl consumers recruited from both fixed and mobile syringe service programs in Gaston and Burke County, North Carolina. Interviews explored sensory discernment strategies, pharmacologic effects, and behavioral responses to the presence of xylazine. Data were analyzed using a combined deductive-inductive thematic approach in QSR NVivo 14.0. Results: Participants described a distinctive repertoire of sensory strategies for identifying xylazine in their fentanyl supply, including the appearance of drug residue on foil, bitterness and chemical odor when smoked, and altered viscosity when injected. A minority described an inability to detect xylazine through sensory cues. Participants consistently distinguished a profound involuntary sedation they called tranq sleep from the familiar opioid nod, characterizing it by nearly instantaneous loss of consciousness with severe withdrawal upon awakening. While nearly all participants expressed strong aversion to xylazine, a meaningful minority valued its amplifying effects to improve a diminishing fentanyl high. Conclusions: This study offers among the first qualitative description of xylazine exposure in a rural fentanyl market. Findings extend the xylazine literature geographically and pharmacologically and underscore the urgency of harm reduction responses tailored to the distinctive harms of xylazine. In particular, adverse health outcomes that accumulate during episodes of protracted and unarousable sedation, including physical injury, victimization, and the severe withdrawal syndrome that follows upon awakening.

papers.title: The impact of menstruation-related symptoms on women's quality of life, work productivity, and economic burden: a structured narrative review.
papers.abstract: Menstruation-related disorders, including dysmenorrhoea, premenstrual syndrome (PMS)/ premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), and heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB)/ abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB), are common among women of reproductive age and associated with impairments in quality of life (QOL), mental health, and daily functioning. Increasing evidence indicates that these conditions adversely affect academic and work productivity, with presenteeism constituting a major component of the economic burden. However, the existing evidence remains fragmented. We conducted a structured narrative review supported by a targeted literature search of PubMed and Scopus. Studies published in English between January 2014 and December 2025 were considered if they included female individuals aged 14-59 years and examined menstruation-related symptoms in relation to QOL, work productivity, academic or occupational functioning, or economic outcomes. Because of heterogeneity in study designs, populations, and outcome measures, findings were synthesised thematically rather than quantitatively pooled. A total of 86 studies were used to inform the thematic synthesis. Across conditions, menstruation-related disorders were consistently associated with reduced health-related QOL, psychological distress, and impaired academic and occupational functioning. Productivity loss was observed across disorders and predominantly driven by presenteeism rather than by absenteeism. Dysmenorrhoea and PMS/PMDD were associated with both absenteeism and presenteeism, whereas HMB/AUB was strongly associated with work impairment, which is frequently mediated by anaemia-related symptoms. Psychological distress, including anxiety, depressive symptoms, emotional dysregulation, and sleep disturbance, has emerged as a key contributor to QOL impairment across age groups and regions. Lifestyle factors appeared to modify symptom severity and functional impact. Although treatment and medical consultations often improved symptoms, productivity gains were inconsistent. This review highlights the multidimensional burden of menstruation-related disorders extending from physical symptoms to mental health and functional outcomes. The predominance of presenteeism suggested that conventional metrics based on absenteeism underestimate the true societal impact. The observed gap between symptom improvement and functional recovery underscored the need for integrated approaches that could address both clinical and psychosocial pathways.
